title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Estimation error of the subspace grows with dimension-to-sample ratio, and real activations behave differently from theory, defining a high-ratio regime.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared axes, red vertical line and shaded regime in last
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the same axes. The x-axis is dimensionality over sample size (d/N) on a log scale from 10^-1 to 10^2. The y-axis is principal subspace angle in degrees, from 0 to 90. Panel (a) shows a blue synthetic spiked-covariance PCA curve that rises and saturates near 80 degrees. A grey dashed horizontal line marks the D-K bound. Panel (b) shows orange square (AG News) and green triangle (SST-2) BERT-base curves that rise roughly linearly to about 52 degrees. Panel (c) overlays the faded blue synthetic curve with the two BERT curves. A pink shaded region labeled 'High-d/N regime' starts at d/N≈10. A dotted red vertical line at d/N=10 appears in every panel. Error bars are small. The eye goes first to the rising curves and then to the red line and shaded region.
caption: PCA estimation error vs. d/N. (a) Synthetic spiked covariance. (b) BERT-base [CLS] activations on AG News and SST-2. (c) Overlay. The shaded region marks the empirical high-d/N regime associated with the largest direction-aware gains in our experiments. Error bars show ±1 std.
abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $Ï$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.
